title: Quiz — which of Verne's club details is real?
learning_goal: Know that Verne's Reform is half fantasy (porphyry columns, blue glass) and half exact (nine garden windows); know you can visit during Open House.

narration.script: Verne describes the inside of the club with much detail. Mosaic floors. A gallery under a dome, held up by twenty red stone columns. Blue painted windows. A dining room with nine windows onto a garden. Compare that with Barry's real building. Which of these details is real? Take your time; the tea is famous.
narration.after_script: Half invented, half exact — read the novel that way for the next seventy-nine days. One practical note. You can stand in that hall yourself, one weekend a year, on the club's Open House London tours. The dates are in the caption. The tour, they say, has one very long staircase.

interaction.prompt: Verne describes the Reform Club's interior. Which of these details is real?

options.text: Twenty red porphyry Ionic columns holding up a dome
options.feedback: Verne's invention. Barry's saloon has a two-storey peristyle — Ionic below, Corinthian above — in scagliola made to look like dark Siena marble.

options.text: A gallery lit through blue painted windows
options.feedback: A garble. The saloon sits under a coved glass roof with an oval saucer-dome.

options.text: A dining-room with nine windows onto the garden
options.feedback: Exact. Nine tall casement windows in the coffee-room's south wall, and the garden is still there.

transition.music_cue: M-43 out under the last line

production_notes: Question ≈ 20 s (narration.script), then the guide PAUSES (pause_narration) until the traveller answers or 30 s elapse (timeout_s); the option feedback shows; then narration.after_script (≈ 25 s) plays. The Open House date lives on the caption only so it can be updated yearly (F-17 is time-sensitive; D9). Linear cut: the guide asks and answers in one breath (script + correct option + its feedback + after_script), ~65 s; keep the prompt overlay.

So the honest fix was to delete the dead row, not to substitute a prettier dead row. M-23 keeps the slot, and its note now records the one-image rule so the next pass does not re-add a 'backdrop'.
